questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What Makes the Membrane Fluid
questions.learningObjective: explain what the fluid part of the fluid mosaic model predicts for membrane proteins
questions.stem: A small region of a living cell membrane is bleached with a strong light and then watched without further damage. Fluorescence returns to the bleached patch over a few seconds, and the molecules are never damaged. What does the return of fluorescence show?

options.text: Proteins move sideways within the plane of the membrane, which is the fluid part
The membrane is rebuilt in place, so fresh protein is laid down over the bleached area
options.misconception: believes photobleaching removes material that the cell then has to replace

options.text: The bilayer is fluid, so each protein is fluid and shapeless and cannot hold a fixed shape
options.misconception: assumes fluidity of the lipid means the protein loses its own structure

options.text: Water refills the bleached patch by osmosis, carrying the fluorescent label with it back
options.misconception: explains protein movement as bulk water flow rather than protein diffusion

questions.explanation: Fluorescence returning means unbleached proteins have moved into the darkened region, so the label is travelling sideways inside the plane of the membrane. Fluidity of the bilayer lets proteins diffuse laterally, which is the half of the model this technique tests. The tempting belief that the membrane simply repairs itself fails because the bleached molecules are intact and merely out of the spotlit region, and the belief that a fluid bilayer makes the protein shapeless fails because each protein keeps its own folded structure; only its position changes. Sideways diffusion is the common case, while flipping from one leaflet to the other is rare and needs enzymes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the label is being rebuilt, moved, or carried by water.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What Selectively Permeable Adds
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a selectively permeable membrane from a simple sieve
questions.stem: One membrane lets water through but stops glucose, while another lets glucose through but stops water. What does the description selectively permeable add on top of a plain sieve?

options.text: Passage depends on which solute is present, not only on the size of any opening
Passage is settled by pore size alone, so a bigger solute is always the one blocked
options.misconception: assumes a sieve model in which size is the only variable that matters

options.text: The membrane admits solutes at random, so each solute gets through about half the time
options.misconception: believes selectivity means a random fifty-fifty admission rate for every solute

options.text: The cell switches each solute on or off at will, with a separate gate for each one
options.misconception: believes selectivity implies conscious control of every solute separately

questions.explanation: Selectivity means the decision to admit depends on the identity of the solute, through polarity, size and the presence of a protein route, not on a single physical hole. The two membranes in the question show the same idea twice: the first passes the small polar molecule and rejects the large one, the second does the reverse, so no single size threshold can explain both. The tempting belief that size alone decides fails because the second membrane lets a large solute through while blocking a small one. The belief that selectivity is a coin toss fails because a rejected solute crosses far less often than an admitted one, and the belief about deliberate gating fails because selectivity is a property of the membrane, not a decision taken by the cell.
questions.hint: Compare the two membranes: what single rule could produce both outcomes?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Net and Gross Movement at Equilibrium
questions.learningObjective: explain why no net movement still allows continued molecular movement
questions.stem: A solute has diffused between two connected compartments until their concentrations are equal, and no further net movement is recorded. Which statement is still true at that point?

options.text: Molecules keep crossing in both directions, but at matching rates so there is no net gain
All movement has now stopped, and the molecules have been locked into a single compartment
options.misconception: believes a stop in net movement means every molecule has stopped as well

options.text: Molecules keep moving, but now only from the dilute side towards the concentrated side
options.misconception: believes a random walk develops a preferred direction once the levels are equal

options.text: Molecules have joined the membrane permanently, so the compartment can no longer exchange them
options.misconception: believes molecules in a membrane are locked into it rather than crossing it

questions.explanation: Equality of concentration is a dynamic equilibrium, not a static one: random thermal motion keeps pushing molecules across the membrane, and the two opposing fluxes are equal, so the measured change is zero while the movement is not. The tempting belief that the molecules have settled down fails because temperature keeps them in motion, and the belief that a direction then develops fails because a random walk with no preference has no preferred outcome. This matters physiologically because it is the two-way leak that makes a resting potential possible: a small steady leak in each direction can still leave a net difference in charge.
questions.hint: Distinguish what a measurement of change can show from what is actually happening.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Osmosis Is Defined by Its Solvent
questions.learningObjective: identify the substance whose movement makes a process osmosis
questions.stem: A tissue cell is bathed in pure water and its own cytoplasm holds a richer mixture of dissolved solutes, so water runs in until the membrane resists further entry. Why is that called osmosis rather than the diffusion of a solute?

options.text: The substance that moves is the solvent water, not a solute travelling down a gradient
It is called osmosis because only a solvent can ever cross a selectively permeable membrane
options.misconception: believes solutes are physically unable to cross any selectively permeable membrane

options.text: It is called osmosis because the cell is pumping the water in with a carrier protein of its own
options.misconception: believes water entry is an active process rather than a passive one

options.text: It is called osmosis because water moves here and solutes always use facilitated transport
options.misconception: believes solutes can only cross by facilitated transport and water cannot

questions.explanation: Osmosis is the net movement of the solvent, which in a cell is water, across a membrane that is more permeable to it than to the solute. The cell is the more concentrated compartment, so water enters down its own gradient until the pressures balance. The tempting belief that the name flags the membrane rather than the substance fails because solutes cross selectively permeable membranes all the time, in both directions. The belief that a pump drives water in fails because no energy is consumed; water moves passively, and a cell in pure water is closer to bursting than to being rescued by a pump.
questions.hint: Name the substance that is actually moving across the membrane.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What a Carrier Contributes
questions.learningObjective: explain what a carrier adds for a solute that cannot cross the lipid core
questions.stem: Glucose is polar and carries a shell of water molecules around it, so entering the membrane's oily core would cost it that shell. What does a carrier protein contribute that the bare bilayer cannot?

options.text: A hydrophilic route through the core, so the solute never has to enter the lipid interior
Extra lipid within the membrane that makes the whole core temporarily water soluble
options.misconception: believes the carrier works by dissolving the solute in the lipid instead of avoiding it

options.text: An active pump that spends ATP to drag the solute across, the only way it can move
options.misconception: conflates a carrier with a pump and denies that the solute can move passively

options.text: A wide gap in the bilayer whose size is set by the largest solute that has to pass
options.misconception: reduces a carrier to a hole and ignores the binding and shape change it performs

questions.explanation: A polar solute cannot dissolve through a nonpolar core, so a carrier or channel provides a lined passage that is hydrophilic inside, allowing the solute to be held by protein groups and released on the far side. The carrier also binds specifically, which is why a glucose carrier will not carry an amino acid. The tempting belief that the carrier dissolves the solute in the lipid fails because lipid is the barrier, not the route. The belief that a carrier is by definition an ATP-driven pump fails because carriers come in both forms, and this one moves the solute only down its gradient. The belief that it is a wide gap fails because a carrier alternates between two shapes around a bound solute rather than leaving an open hole.
questions.hint: Ask whether the solute ever enters the lipid part of the membrane.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What Active Transport Buys
questions.learningObjective: explain why moving a solute against its gradient requires an energy source
questions.stem: A cell moves sodium ions from where they are already scarce to where they are already abundant. What must that process spend, and what does the spending accomplish?

options.text: Chemical energy from ATP, which pays for the work of concentrating the ions uphill
No energy at all, because the ions happen to be moving down their own concentration gradient
options.misconception: believes uphill movement is free when the charge gradient is ignored

options.text: Heat from respiration, which pushes the ions uphill by stretching the membrane further
options.misconception: believes thermal energy is converted directly into directed ion movement

options.text: Chemical energy from ATP, which is consumed only to move the water that follows the ions
options.misconception: mislabels what the ATP is spent on and leaves the ion uphill unexplained

questions.explanation: Concentrating a solute where it is already abundant stores potential energy in the gradient, and no passive route can do that, because passive movement only runs downhill. The energy comes from ATP, which is hydrolysed by the transport protein as the solute is moved, so the work appears as a gradient that can later be released to do useful work. The tempting belief that the movement is free fails because the two gradients oppose each other: the chemical gradient pushes one way and the electrical gradient the other, and something must supply the difference. The belief that heat does it fails because heat is disordered and cannot drive a specific solute one way. The belief that ATP is spent on water fails because water follows the ions by osmosis rather than by hydrolysis.
questions.hint: Ask what work is being done here that passive movement cannot do.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Two Conditions for a Membrane Potential
questions.learningObjective: state the two requirements for a voltage difference to persist across a membrane
questions.stem: A membrane holds a voltage difference across itself, with the inside negative relative to the outside. Which two conditions must both hold for that difference to persist rather than collapse?

options.text: The ion distribution is unequal, and the membrane is not equally permeable to those ions
The ion distribution is equal, and the membrane is equally permeable to every ion present
options.misconception: believes a uniform distribution and uniform permeability can still hold a charge difference

options.text: The ion distribution is unequal, and the membrane lets every ion cross with no restriction
options.misconception: believes an unrestricted membrane can still hold a steady voltage difference

options.text: The ion distribution is equal, and the membrane blocks all charged particles from passing
options.misconception: pairs equal distribution with a closed membrane and calls the result a potential

questions.explanation: Two things are needed at once. First, unequal distribution puts a chemical gradient to work, and second, unequal permeability stops the ions from simply running back down that gradient, so the imbalance of charge is maintained rather than erased. The tempting belief that an equal distribution works fails because with no gradient there is no driving force, and the belief that a fully open membrane works fails because an unrestricted membrane short-circuits and collapses towards zero. The pair with equal distribution and a closed membrane describes a capacitor rather than a living cell, because a blocked membrane can hold a voltage only while a charge is placed on it by some separate process.
questions.hint: Ask what supplies the driving force, and what stops it running out.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why Resting Potential Sits Near the Potassium Balance
questions.learningObjective: explain why the resting potential is nearer one ion's equilibrium value than the other's
questions.stem: At rest the membrane potential of a cell sits far closer to the value that potassium alone would give than to the one that sodium alone would give. Which property of the resting membrane explains that position?

options.text: Its permeability to potassium is far greater than its permeability to sodium at rest
Its permeability to potassium is far smaller than its permeability to sodium at rest
options.misconception: reverses the relative permeabilities that decide which ion dominates the rest

options.text: Potassium is pumped out continuously, so the charge outside carries the voltage instead
options.misconception: attributes the resting potential to a pump rather than to permeability

options.text: The two equilibrium values are identical, so the position between them is purely arbitrary
options.misconception: believes both ions predict the same resting potential and the real value is a guess

questions.explanation: The resting potential is a weighted compromise between the equilibrium values that each ion would impose, and the weights are the membrane's relative permeabilities. Because the resting membrane is far more permeable to potassium than to sodium, potassium dominates and pulls the value most of the way towards its own equilibrium potential, while the small sodium leak keeps it from arriving there exactly. The tempting belief that the permeabilities are reversed fails because that would place the value nearer the sodium side. The belief that a pump creates the resting potential fails because the pump maintains the concentration gradients over hours while the voltage responds to permeability within milliseconds. The belief that the two values coincide fails because they differ by well over a hundred millivolts.
questions.hint: Think of the resting potential as a compromise weighted by how easily each ion gets through.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: The Threshold Potential
questions.learningObjective: explain what changes when a membrane reaches its threshold potential
questions.stem: Repeated stimuli depolarise a neuron by small amounts, and one of them finally brings the membrane to a critical voltage. What happens at that critical voltage that had not been happening before?

options.text: Enough voltage-gated sodium channels open to start a self-amplifying feedback loop
The membrane becomes freely permeable to every ion until the cell fully equilibrates with outside
options.misconception: believes threshold ends the barrier and lets all ions mix at once

options.text: The transmitter already in the gap is suddenly released in a much larger quantity
options.misconception: confuses a change in the receiving membrane with a change at the nerve ending

options.text: The axon stops conducting and the resting voltage is restored immediately instead
options.misconception: believes threshold triggers inhibition rather than the firing of an impulse

questions.explanation: Below threshold, the depolarisation stays graded: it rises with the size of the stimulus and fades away again, because the small inward current does not regenerate itself. At threshold, enough voltage-gated sodium channels are open that sodium entry depolarises still further, which opens more of them, and the loop runs away to the full amplitude of the impulse regardless of how small the triggering stimulus was. That is why the amplitude of an impulse does not code for stimulus strength. The tempting belief that threshold lets all ions mix fails because the channels involved are selective and the impulse ends well short of equilibrium. The belief about transmitter release fails because the ending has usually already discharged by the time the impulse reaches it.
questions.hint: Ask what makes the depolarisation keep going once it starts.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Releasing Transmitter at a Nerve Ending
questions.learningObjective: sequence the events that release a neurotransmitter from a nerve ending
questions.stem: An action potential arrives at the terminal of a nerve ending that is packed with small membrane-bound packets. Which sequence gets the contents of those packets out into the gap?

options.text: The terminal depolarises, calcium enters, and the packets fuse with the surface and empty
The terminal hyperpolarises, sodium exits, and the packets fuse with the wall and empty
options.misconception: puts the ending in the wrong electrical state and the wrong membrane in the way

options.text: The contents leak across on their own, and calcium enters afterwards to complete the release
options.misconception: reverses the order, so release happens before the trigger that causes it

options.text: The terminal contracts and squeezes the packets open, after which calcium leaves the ending
options.misconception: describes a mechanical expulsion and the wrong direction of calcium movement

questions.explanation: The arriving impulse depolarises the terminal, which opens channels that let calcium in, and the rise in calcium inside is the trigger that makes vesicles move to the surface, fuse with it, and empty their contents outwards by exocytosis. Calcium is the switch because it is the local signal that converts an electrical event into a mechanical one at the membrane. The tempting belief that hyperpolarisation precedes release fails because the terminal must be depolarised for the calcium channels to open. The belief that contents leak first fails because a charged transmitter would not cross the bilayer unassisted, and calcium is upstream, not downstream. The belief that contraction squeezes the vesicles open fails because vesicle release is membrane fusion, not muscular squeezing.
questions.hint: Start from the electrical event, and name the ion that acts as the internal switch.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Ending a Neurotransmitter's Action
questions.learningObjective: explain why neurotransmitter removal sets the timing of a signal
questions.stem: A target cell must be free to respond again as soon as possible, so a signal between two cells cannot be allowed to persist. Which set of processes keeps a neurotransmitter's action short?

options.text: Reuptake into the nerve ending, breakdown by enzymes in the gap, or diffusion away
Continued release from the ending, widening of the gap, and slow receptor insertion
options.misconception: believes persistence of the signal comes from releasing more and spreading it further

options.text: Uptake into the target cell, thickening of the membrane, and delayed receptor closure
options.misconception: believes the target cell swallowing the transmitter prolongs rather than ends the signal

options.text: Freezing inside packets, coating with receptor protein, and drifting along the membrane
options.misconception: believes transmitter is immobilised and made longer-lived rather than cleared away

questions.explanation: A synapse has no inherent off switch, so the signal is ended by removing the transmitter itself: pumping it back into the ending, chopping it up with enzymes, or letting it diffuse away. That is what makes synaptic transmission fast, and a drug that blocks one of these routes produces a prolonged signal, which is a useful clue about which step it attacks. The tempting belief that persistence comes from more release fails because the problem is how to stop, not how to continue. The belief that the target cell's uptake prolongs the signal fails because uptake removes the transmitter from the cleft. The belief that freezing or coating preserves it fails because both make the molecule harder to remove.
questions.hint: Ask what has to disappear from the gap for the next signal to work.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Excitatory and Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potentials
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the ion channel behaviour behind an excitatory and an inhibitory potential
questions.stem: One synapse makes a target neuron slightly more likely to fire, and another makes it slightly less likely. What difference at the receptor channel produces these opposite effects?

options.text: The first opens channels carrying positive charge in, the second channels carrying charge out
The first acts faster, and the second acts slower but produces an exactly equal effect
options.misconception: believes the sign of the effect comes from the speed rather than from the ions

options.text: The first needs more transmitter, and the second needs a chemically different transmitter
options.misconception: believes the two effects are distinguished only by the amount or type of transmitter

options.text: The first acts on the nerve ending, and the second acts on the transmitter before release
options.misconception: places both effects on the sending side of the synapse rather than the receiving one

questions.explanation: Both effects are produced by ligand-gated channels, and what differs is the charge of the ions they pass. Channels that admit sodium and calcium let positive charge in, moving the membrane voltage towards threshold, while channels that admit chloride or potassium move charge in the opposite direction or let positive charge leave, moving the voltage away from threshold. Neither effect is all or nothing, which is why they are graded and can be added together. The tempting belief that speed decides the sign fails because a slow inhibitory input is still inhibitory. The belief that amount or identity of transmitter decides fails because the same transmitter can be excitatory at one receptor and inhibitory at another, depending on the channel it opens. The belief that the effect is on the sending side fails because the graded change is in the receiving membrane.
questions.hint: Ask which way the charge moves when each channel opens.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Summation of Many Weak Inputs
questions.learningObjective: explain how weak synaptic inputs combine into a single firing decision
questions.stem: A neuron receives several hundred small excitatory inputs each second, and none of them is strong enough to fire it alone. What property of the neuron lets the total produce a single clear decision?

options.text: The inputs add together in space and in time, and the summed value is compared with threshold
Each input is amplified at its own synapse until it reaches threshold independently of the rest
options.misconception: believes every synapse amplifies enough to fire the cell on its own

options.text: The weakest inputs are discarded and only the largest single one is passed along to the axon
options.misconception: believes the neuron selects one winner rather than adding the inputs up

options.text: The inputs are sorted by size and passed on only when they arrive in the correct time order
options.misconception: believes the decision depends on arrival order rather than on the sum of the effect

questions.explanation: The graded changes produced at synapses add together, both across many synapses at once and over time at a single one, and it is the total at the initial segment that is compared with threshold. This is why one strong input, several weak ones arriving together, and a rapid train all produce the same result. The tempting belief that each synapse amplifies enough on its own fails because a typical excitatory input is far too small to reach threshold, which is the normal condition rather than an exception. The belief that the neuron picks a single winner fails because nothing is discarded before the sum is taken. The belief that order decides fails because the sum is over magnitude, not sequence, though timing affects whether the effects overlap in time.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to several small voltage changes before the cell fires.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: The One-to-One Nerve to Muscle Relationship
questions.learningObjective: explain why a nerve impulse reliably produces one muscle impulse
questions.stem: At the junction between a motor nerve and a muscle fibre, one nerve impulse reliably produces one muscle impulse and not a variable number. What accounts for that dependable pairing?

options.text: Each impulse releases a fixed amount of transmitter that reliably carries the muscle past threshold
Each impulse releases a fixed amount that never quite brings the muscle up to its threshold
options.misconception: believes the safety margin is negative and the muscle responds by luck

options.text: The muscle responds only to transmitter that has already been broken down by an enzyme
options.misconception: believes muscle responds to the breakdown product rather than the transmitter

options.text: The nerve keeps releasing transmitter until the muscle fires, then stops immediately afterwards
options.misconception: believes the muscle's response controls the release rather than the other way round

questions.explanation: The amount of transmitter released by a single impulse is large enough to drive the end-plate potential well past the muscle's threshold, so the muscle fires every time, which is called the safety factor. That is also why a nerve impulse produces a single muscle impulse rather than a graded response, since the all-or-none property takes over once threshold is passed. The tempting belief that the amount falls short fails because the junction is built with a large margin, and insufficient release produces a weak contraction rather than a reliably graded one. The belief that the muscle responds to the breakdown product fails because enzymes act on the transmitter to end the signal. The belief that release continues until the muscle fires fails because nothing travels back from the muscle to the nerve ending to do that.
questions.hint: Ask how far past the muscle's threshold the end-plate potential is driven.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Separating a Hormone from a Neurotransmitter
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a hormone from a neurotransmitter by route and reach
questions.stem: One signal molecule is secreted into the blood by an endocrine cell and reaches a target organ some distance away. Which feature separates it from a neurotransmitter?

options.text: It travels through the circulation and acts on the cells that carry a matching receptor
It travels only across a narrow gap and acts on the cell immediately opposite it
options.misconception: describes a neurotransmitter and gives no distinguishing feature for a hormone

options.text: It is built from cholesterol and cannot be broken down, so its effect never ends quickly
options.misconception: gives the hormone a nonexistent stability and a wrong building material

options.text: It enters the target nucleus and rewrites the sequence of that cell's structural genes
options.misconception: confuses a hormone signal with a direct change to the DNA sequence itself

questions.explanation: Both are chemical signals and both act by binding a receptor, so the difference is how they travel and how far they reach. A hormone enters the blood and reaches any cell anywhere in the body that has the right receptor, so its effects depend on which tissues express that receptor; a neurotransmitter is released at a specific ending into a gap of a few micrometres and acts on the cell opposite. Hormone effects are also slower to start and longer lasting, which is what makes the two systems suit different jobs. The tempting belief that only a neurotransmitter crosses a gap fails because that is a property of a route, not of a molecule class. The belief about cholesterol and permanence fails because steroid hormones are made from cholesterol but are broken down normally. The belief about rewriting genes fails because a hormone acts through second messengers, not by altering the sequence.
questions.hint: Compare the route each takes between the cell that makes it and the cell that responds.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why Only Some Cells Answer a Hormone
questions.learningObjective: explain what determines which target cells respond to a circulating hormone
questions.stem: A hormone circulates in the blood and passes within touching distance of nearly every cell in the body, yet only some of them respond. What decides which cells answer?

options.text: Whether the cell carries a receptor that binds the hormone and can signal from it
Whether the cell happens to lie nearest the gland that released the hormone first
options.misconception: believes the nearest cells to the gland are the privileged targets of a hormone

options.text: Whether the cell has a large enough nucleus to hold a copy of the hormone's message
options.misconception: believes the message is a physical molecule that must be stored in a nucleus

options.text: Whether the cell is dividing at that moment, since only dividing cells read signals
options.misconception: believes a hormone can only be heard by a cell that is currently dividing

questions.explanation: Circulating hormones are exposed to everything in the blood, so the only way to be selective is for responding cells to be the ones expressing a matching receptor with a working signalling pathway behind it. This is why one hormone can speed up the heart, change liver glucose output and alter kidney reabsorption at the same time, while cells without that receptor ignore it. The tempting belief that proximity to the gland matters fails because the hormone is diluted long before it arrives and travels to every part of the circulation. The belief about nuclear storage fails because the hormone does not need to be stored in the cell at all; it stays outside and binds a receptor. The belief about dividing cells fails because receptor expression, not cell division, decides sensitivity, and many target cells are not dividing.
questions.hint: Ask what a cell must possess before it can respond at all.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Negative Feedback in a Control Loop
questions.learningObjective: describe how a negative feedback loop corrects a disturbance from a set point
questions.stem: A quantity such as body temperature is held near a set value by a control loop with a sensor, a controller, an effector and a signal back from the result. Which description is that loop working correctly?

options.text: A rise triggers responses that oppose the rise, so the deviation is driven back to the set point
A rise triggers responses that add to the rise, so the deviation grows until a limit is reached
options.misconception: describes a positive feedback loop and calls it the correct one

options.text: A rise triggers responses that act only once the value has already returned to normal
options.misconception: describes a loop that waits for the outcome instead of correcting it

options.text: A rise triggers responses that move the set point itself, so a new normal becomes the target
options.misconception: believes the loop defends a fixed set point rather than the point that can move

questions.explanation: A negative feedback loop is one whose response opposes the deviation, so it reduces the error between the measured value and the set point and then the response fades as the error disappears. That is why the loop settles rather than oscillating, and why the correction is automatic once the sensor reports the change. The tempting belief that a rise should add to itself fails because that is a positive loop, which is right for processes that must run to completion and wrong for ones that must return to a value. The belief that the loop acts only after recovery fails because then it could not prevent the deviation from becoming dangerous. The belief that the set point moves fails because that is a separate idea, more like resetting a target during illness, and it is not what makes a loop negative.
questions.hint: Ask whether the response adds to the deviation or takes it away.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why a Positive Feedback Loop Is Useful
questions.learningObjective: explain why some processes need a positive rather than a negative feedback loop
questions.stem: During childbirth each contraction strengthens the hormone release that provoked it, and the effect feeds itself. Why would a body build in a loop like this rather than a restoring one?

options.text: Some processes must run to completion, so amplifying the effect is needed rather than holding a value
Amplifying loops are needed because restoring loops cannot be made sensitive enough to detect change
options.misconception: believes restoring loops are inadequate sensors rather than the wrong shape for the job

options.text: All control is amplifying, and the restoring pattern is a story written after the event
options.misconception: denies negative feedback and treats it as a retrospective invention

options.text: It works only because the hormone is cleared slowly, so its effect builds up over the whole birth
options.misconception: explains an amplifying loop as slow clearance rather than as a designed amplifier

questions.explanation: A restoring loop is right for keeping a variable near a value, but it is useless for a process that has to go from nothing to a large threshold and then stop, because as soon as the effect began to approach the target a restoring loop would oppose it. An amplifying loop solves that by pushing the effect away from itself, so contractions must grow until the birth is complete, at which point the hormone release falls and the loop stops. Clotting and the surge of luteinising hormone before ovulation work the same way. The tempting belief that restoring loops are bad sensors fails because detection is a separate matter from the sign of the response. The belief that all control is amplifying fails because most of the body's variables are held steady. The belief that slow clearance explains it fails because clearance only changes the timescale, not the sign of the response.
questions.hint: Ask whether the process needs to return to a value or to be driven all the way to an endpoint.

questions.stem: A runner's core temperature rises during a race on a hot day and the sweating rate goes up. What physical process does the sweat perform, and what kind of loop does the response belong to?

options.text: Evaporation removes heat, so the response opposes the rise in a negative feedback loop
Sweat absorbs heat from the skin into the droplets, which then warm the body further
options.misconception: believes liquid sweat carries heat into the body rather than out of it

options.text: Evaporation removes heat, so the response amplifies the rise in a positive feedback loop
options.misconception: keeps the mechanism right but calls the sign of the response positive

options.text: Sweat lowers the temperature directly, so the loop has neither a sensor nor a set point
options.misconception: believes sweating acts without any sensor driving it and removes the loop

questions.explanation: Sweat only cools the body when it evaporates, because the molecules need the energy for the change of state, and that energy is drawn from the skin. The controller detects the rising core temperature and increases sweating and widens skin blood vessels, both of which increase heat loss, so the response opposes the disturbance and the loop is negative. The tempting belief that liquid sweat warms the body fails because the droplets only take heat away once they evaporate, and dripping sweat removes little. The belief that the response amplifies the rise fails because cooling opposes the rise, and the loop stops as the temperature returns. The belief that there is no sensor fails because a controller comparing the measured value with a set point is exactly what turns a temperature change into a response.
questions.hint: Ask where the energy goes when a sweat droplet evaporates.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why the Vasa Recta Is a Hairpin
questions.learningObjective: explain why counter-current flow preserves a medullary solute gradient
questions.stem: The vasa recta, the blood supply to the kidney's inner medulla, is shaped as a hairpin whose two limbs carry blood in opposite directions. Why does the arrangement have to be that way?

options.text: Opposite flow lets the leaving blood carry away what the arriving blood delivers, so the gradient survives
A hairpin doubles the pressure inside the vessel, which forces more solute out into the medulla
options.misconception: believes the gradient is created by pressure inside a blood vessel

options.text: Opposite flow lets the blood collect the whole solute load that the loop of Henle has discarded
options.misconception: believes the vasa recta builds the gradient by loading up with discarded solute

options.text: A hairpin keeps the blood hot, so the medulla stays warm enough to hold the loop of Henle shut
options.misconception: believes the medullary gradient is a temperature gradient rather than a solute one

questions.explanation: The medulla must stay more concentrated than the surrounding cortex for the kidney to pull water out of the collecting duct, and that gradient is easily destroyed by the blood supply washing it out. A hairpin solves this because the two limbs flow in opposite directions, so the blood leaving the medulla meets the blood entering it and passes solute straight from one to the other instead of carrying it away down a single outflow. The result is that the vasa recta can supply the tissue while removing almost no solute. The tempting belief about pressure fails because a modest pressure rise does not concentrate the interstitium, and the loop of Henle does that work. The belief that the vessel collects discarded solute fails because collecting it would remove it from the medulla rather than build a gradient. The belief about heat fails because the gradient that matters is osmotic, although the same arrangement does limit heat loss as a side effect.
questions.hint: Compare what the blood leaves the medulla carrying with what arrives.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What Drives Filtration at the Glomerulus
questions.learningObjective: explain what drives fluid out of the glomerular capillaries
questions.stem: Fluid and small solutes leave the glomerular capillaries and enter the capsule surrounding them, and no chemical energy is consumed at the point where this happens. What provides the force that drives them across?

options.text: Blood pressure in the capillary, pushing against a filter that holds back cells and large proteins
Carrier proteins spending chemical energy to push fluid from the blood into the capsule
options.misconception: believes filtration is an active transport step performed by carrier proteins

options.text: An osmotic gradient that draws water across, with the solutes following the water passively
options.misconception: believes a solute gradient and no pressure account for the filtered fluid

options.text: An active pump that moves sodium across, with the water and other solutes following the sodium
options.misconception: believes a pressure-driven step depends on a prior pump moving sodium

questions.explanation: Filtration is driven by the hydrostatic pressure of blood in the capillary, which pushes water and small solutes through gaps in the filtration barrier while cells and large proteins are too large to pass. No chemical energy is needed because the process is driven by a pressure difference, not by moving solutes against a gradient. The tempting belief that carriers are involved fails because no transporter participates; the barrier is a physical filter. The belief that an osmotic gradient drives it fails because the two sides are close in solute concentration, so osmosis cannot supply the force. The belief that a pump is a prerequisite fails because the pressure is generated by the heart, and it would keep filtering even if every pump in the tubule were blocked.
questions.hint: Ask what pushes the fluid, not what carries the solutes.

questions.topic: Physiology: Which Segment of the Gut Absorbs
questions.learningObjective: identify the segment where most absorption occurs and what the large intestine takes up
questions.stem: A meal of bread, egg and butter passes along the digestive tract and its components are taken into the body. Which statement about the segments involved is correct?

options.text: Most absorption happens in the small intestine, and the large intestine takes up water and salts
Most absorption happens in the stomach, and the small intestine takes up water alone
options.misconception: moves the main absorptive surface to the stomach and strips the small intestine

options.text: Most absorption happens in the large intestine, and the small intestine takes up water alone
options.misconception: puts the main absorptive surface in the segment that mainly compacts waste

options.text: Absorption is spread evenly across the mouth, stomach, small intestine and large intestine alike
options.misconception: believes every segment absorbs equally and removes the length of the small intestine

questions.explanation: The small intestine is where most absorption happens, because it is long, its lining is thrown into folds and villi that multiply the surface, and it receives pancreatic juice and bile that finish digestion at the same place. What the large intestine takes is mostly what has been left behind: water, salts, and the vitamins made by the bacteria living there. The tempting belief that the stomach absorbs most fails because its lining resists absorption and its job is mechanical churning plus acid and enzyme action. The belief that the small intestine takes up water alone fails because it is where amino acids, sugars and digested fats are absorbed. The belief that absorption is even fails because the segments are built for different jobs.
questions.hint: Match each segment to what it is built to do.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why a Lining Is Folded at Three Scales
questions.learningObjective: explain why nested folds multiply absorptive surface area
questions.stem: A lining is thrown into circular folds, each fold carries finger-like villi, and every villus is covered in a brush border of microvilli. How does that nested arrangement change the absorptive area?

options.text: It multiplies the area at three nested scales, so the total rise is a product of the three factors
It multiplies the area at three nested scales, so the total rise is only the sum of the three
options.misconception: believes the gains from each scale add rather than compound

options.text: It changes the area very little, because each fold removes as much surface as the villi add
options.misconception: believes the folds consume the area that the smaller projections create

options.text: It raises the area only at the largest scale, because the smaller scales are too small to count
options.misconception: believes area gain depends on the size of the feature rather than its number

questions.explanation: Each scale multiplies the gain of the one below it, so a fold with villi, each villus with microvilli, multiplies the starting area by the product of the three factors rather than their sum. That compounding is what lets a short gut absorb as much as it does. The tempting belief that the gains add fails because the features are nested, not side by side, so a villus on a fold occupies area that only exists because the fold is there. The belief that the folds cancel the villi fails because folding is what creates the extra lining to begin with. The belief that only the largest scale matters fails because the number of villi and microvilli is where most of the multiplication happens.
questions.hint: Decide whether the three multipliers are combined by adding or by multiplying.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why the Oxygen Dissociation Curve Is S-Shaped
questions.learningObjective: explain the cooperativity that gives the haemoglobin dissociation curve its shape
questions.stem: The curve relating the partial pressure of oxygen to the percentage of haemoglobin sites that are holding oxygen is S-shaped rather than a straight line. What produces that shape?

options.text: Binding one oxygen makes the remaining sites bind more readily, so the curve steepens then flattens
Each haemoglobin holds exactly one oxygen, and the curve is skewed by mixing two such molecules
options.misconception: assumes a single site and explains the shape by molecule number instead of binding

options.text: The partial pressure rises unevenly as altitude changes, which bends an otherwise linear relation
options.misconception: blames an irregular x axis rather than anything about the binding process itself

options.text: Temperature varies between measurements, which curves a relation that begins perfectly linear
options.misconception: blames the measurement conditions rather than the molecule doing the binding

questions.explanation: Haemoglobin binds cooperatively: the four subunits move together, so the first oxygen makes the remaining sites less reluctant, the curve rises steeply through the middle, and once nearly every site is filled there is nothing left to fill, so the curve flattens. That steep middle section is also what allows haemoglobin to load fully in the lung and release a good fraction in the tissues. The tempting belief that each molecule holds one oxygen fails because there are four sites, and one-oxygen binding would give a hyperbolic rather than an S-shaped curve. The beliefs about altitude and temperature fail because neither changes the relation between pressure and occupancy for a fixed haemoglobin sample.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the remaining sites after the first one is filled.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Reading Osmosis in Three Solutions
questions.learningObjective: use weighings before and after immersion to identify the direction of water movement

stimulus.body: Laboratory note (written for this course): Pieces of the same fresh tissue of equal size are blotted, weighed, and then immersed for thirty minutes in one of three solutions at the same temperature. Solution W is pure water. Solution S has a solute concentration equal to that of the tissue's own sap. Solution H has a solute concentration twice that of the sap. Each piece is re-blotted and weighed after the thirty minutes. The piece in W has gained mass, the piece in S has not changed, and the piece in H has lost mass.

questions.stem: Using only the laboratory note, which set of processes accounts for the three results?

options.text: Osmosis: water entered in W, left in H, and moved neither way in S because the levels were matched
Active transport: the tissue pumped water in W, pumped it out in H, and balanced both flows in S
options.misconception: believes the weight changes come from an energy-driven pump moving water uphill

options.text: Facilitated diffusion: solutes entered in W, left in H, and reached equilibrium in S after thirty minutes
options.misconception: believes the mass change came from solute exchange rather than from water

options.text: Simple diffusion: the tissue lost mass in W, gained mass in H, and changed nothing in S at all
options.misconception: reverses the direction of water movement in both the pure and the concentrated solution

questions.explanation: Water moves across the membrane towards the more concentrated side, so in pure water it enters the tissue and the piece gains mass, in the solution twice as concentrated it leaves and the piece loses mass, and in the matched solution the two sides are balanced so nothing net happens. Mass gain and loss therefore report the direction of water movement without measuring it directly. The tempting belief that a pump is responsible fails because no chemical energy is used and water moves passively. The belief that solutes crossing explains the change fails because the tissue is already in water, and the direction of the change matches water moving rather than solute exchanging. The belief that the directions are reversed fails because water always moves towards the more concentrated compartment, whichever one that is.
questions.hint: Ask which side of the membrane holds more dissolved solute in each of the three beakers.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Locating the Threshold in a Recorded Trace
questions.learningObjective: identify the threshold crossing in a recorded membrane potential trace

stimulus.body: Recording note (written for this course): A fine electrode inside a neuron reports the voltage across its membrane as stimuli of different strengths are applied. At rest the reading is minus seventy millivolts. A weak stimulus moves it to minus sixty, and a slightly stronger one to minus fifty-five, and both then relax back to minus seventy over a second or so. A third stimulus moves the reading to minus thirty within a millisecond, on to plus thirty, then back down past minus fifty, and finally settles near minus seventy. The whole spike occupies about two milliseconds.

questions.stem: Using only the recording note, which step is the one where the threshold is being crossed?

options.text: The step from minus fifty-five to minus thirty, where a graded response becomes self-sustaining
The final return to minus seventy, which is the event that started the earlier rise
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect by treating the recovery as the trigger

options.text: The rise from minus seventy to minus sixty, which is where the first channel opens
options.misconception: mistakes a small graded deflection for the first voltage-gated channel opening

options.text: The jump from minus thirty to plus thirty, which is where the outward current starts
options.misconception: places the start of repolarisation at the peak instead of after the peak

questions.explanation: The two weak stimuli in the note produce small, reversible displacements that relax back on their own, which is the behaviour of a response that never reached threshold. The third stimulus drives the membrane past about minus fifty-five, and from there the depolarisation regenerates itself, producing the fast, full, all-or-none spike described. That step is the crossing. The tempting belief that the recovery started the rise fails because the trace rises first and recovers afterwards. The belief that the first small step is the threshold fails because that deflection faded by itself, and a response that fades is one that never reached threshold. The belief that the peak starts the outward current fails because outward current builds during the fall, not at the top of the rise.
questions.hint: Compare what happened to the two weak stimuli with what happened to the strong one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Reading a Plateau as Carrier Saturation
questions.learningObjective: infer from a rate table that a transported solute uses a finite number of carriers

stimulus.body: Transport note (written for this course): A sheet records the rate at which a solute crosses a cell membrane while the concentration outside is raised. At outside concentrations of 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 units the recorded rates are 8, 15, 24, 32 and 36 units per minute. A second sheet, recorded with a competing solute also present, gives 5, 10, 17, 24 and 27 for the same five concentrations. Doubling the outside concentration from 1 to 2 no longer doubles the rate anywhere in either sheet, and both sheets flatten as the concentration rises further.

questions.stem: Using only the transport note, what does the flattening in the first sheet indicate?

options.text: A finite number of carriers is being occupied, so the rate has a ceiling that more solute cannot raise
The solute has reached the same concentration on both sides, so no net movement remains
options.misconception: reads the flattening as reaching a concentration equilibrium instead of a capacity limit

options.text: The carriers have been damaged by the raised concentration and have stopped working altogether
options.misconception: attributes a smooth plateau to damage rather than to carriers becoming fully occupied

options.text: The membrane has become leaky, so an increasing share of the solute now leaks back outwards
options.misconception: explains the ceiling as a growing reverse leak rather than as limited carrier numbers

questions.explanation: A plateau is the signature of a limited number of transport proteins: once nearly all of them are occupied, adding more solute on the outside cannot be followed by more transport, because the carriers are already working as fast as they can. Simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer has no such ceiling, since it depends only on how many molecules are available to cross. The tempting belief that a concentration equilibrium explains the flattening fails because the outside concentration in the note is still rising, so the two sides are not equal. The belief that damage caused it fails because damage would produce falling rates, not a smooth ceiling. The belief about a growing reverse leak fails because a leak would not produce a reproducible plateau that depends on the number of carriers.
questions.hint: Ask what a membrane with no finite number of carriers would do as the concentration rose.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Reading a Concentration Gradient Along a Nephron
questions.learningObjective: read a four-point concentration table and describe what the kidney achieved

stimulus.body: Renal note (written for this course): Fluid is sampled at four points along a single nephron and its solute concentration is measured in millimoles per litre. Blood plasma entering the glomerulus reads 300. The fluid at the end of the descending limb reads 600. The fluid leaving the ascending limb back in the cortex reads 100. The final urine leaving the collecting duct reads 1,200. The same nephron is sampled again after the patient is given no fluid and a hormone that raises water reabsorption in the collecting duct is released, and the final urine then reads 1,500.

questions.stem: Using only the renal note, which single statement is consistent with all of the readings?

options.text: The loop of Henle and the collecting duct together make the final urine several times concentrated
The kidney filters plasma and passes the same concentration straight through with no change at all
options.misconception: ignores a difference of four times between the entering plasma and the final urine

options.text: The descending limb concentrates the fluid and the ascending limb concentrates it a second time
options.misconception: claims both limbs concentrate, when the ascending limb is seen to dilute the fluid

options.text: The collecting duct dilutes the fluid, so that the final urine matches the plasma it came from
options.misconception: assigns dilution to the duct and ignores the much higher final reading

questions.explanation: The table shows three distinct steps: the filtrate leaves at the plasma concentration, doubles as it descends into the medulla, is diluted to roughly a third of plasma on the way back up, and is then concentrated again on the way out, reaching four times plasma at the end and rising further when water reabsorption is increased. Only a statement that puts the concentrating work in the loop and the duct fits all four readings. The tempting belief that nothing changes fails because the final reading is four times the starting one. The belief that both limbs concentrate fails because the ascending limb measurably dilutes, which is exactly what allows a gradient to be built. The belief that the duct dilutes fails because the duct reading is the highest in the table, and the hormone note shows it can be pushed higher still.
questions.hint: Follow the four numbers in order and ask which segment raised each one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What a Counter-Current Arrangement Multiplies
questions.learningObjective: compare two flow arrangements and identify the multiplication produced by counter-current flow

stimulus.body: Tubular note (written for this course): A single loop of Henle from an isolated kidney is perfused at a fixed flow rate with fluid of 300 millimoles per litre, and the osmolarity of the interstitium immediately around it is then measured. In one preparation the descending and ascending limbs run side by side in the same direction, and the surrounding interstitium is left at 340 millimoles per litre. The same loop is then re-perfused with the limbs running in opposite directions, and the interstitium is left at 1,200 millimoles per litre. Perfusing rate, fluid composition and temperature are held the same in both preparations.

questions.stem: Using only the tubular note, what does the second arrangement demonstrate about the two limbs acting together?

options.text: Running the limbs in opposite directions multiplies a gradient that neither could sustain alone
Running the limbs in opposite directions leaves a lower interstitium than running them together
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the measured difference between the arrangements

options.text: The higher interstitium comes from the loop using more energy when the limbs run backwards
options.misconception: attributes the effect to an energy cost rather than to the geometry of the flow

options.text: The higher interstitium comes from water being pushed out of the interstitium into the loop
options.misconception: explains a solute gradient as a water movement, which the reversed direction of the limb makes impossible

questions.explanation: In the second arrangement the descending limb delivers solute into the interstitium while the ascending limb carries it away, and because the two flow in opposite directions the solute that the ascending limb removes is delivered straight to the descending limb instead of being flushed out of the kidney. Repeated along the length of the loop, that small exchange is multiplied, which is why a gradient that a single passage could never reach appears at all. The tempting belief that the directions are reversed fails because the note measures 340 one way and 1,200 the other. The belief that energy is consumed fails because no chemical energy is spent and the note holds everything else constant. The belief about water being pushed out fails because the ascending limb moves solute out and water in, so the fluid there is the most dilute part of the system.
questions.hint: Ask where the solute leaves the ascending limb goes when the two limbs point opposite ways.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Computing pH from Bicarbonate and Carbon Dioxide
questions.learningObjective: compute the direction of a pH change from a bicarbonate and carbon dioxide pair

stimulus.body: Measurement note (written for this course): Blood is sampled from a person at rest and then again during heavy exercise, and three values are reported for each sample. The relation used to check the readings is that pH equals 6.1 plus the logarithm of the bicarbonate concentration divided by 0.03 times the carbon dioxide partial pressure. Resting sample: bicarbonate 24 millimoles per litre, carbon dioxide partial pressure 40 millimetres of mercury, pH 7.40. Exercising sample: bicarbonate 14, carbon dioxide partial pressure 50, pH 7.07. Applying the relation to the resting pair returns 7.40, and applying it to the exercising pair returns 7.07.

questions.stem: Using only the measurement note, what produced the lower pH in the exercising sample?

options.text: The bicarbonate concentration fell, so the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide shrank
The bicarbonate concentration rose steeply, so the ratio grew and the pH must then have risen
options.misconception: contradicts the reported value and reverses the effect of more bicarbonate

options.text: The carbon dioxide partial pressure fell steeply, so the ratio grew and the pH must have fallen
options.misconception: reverses the effect of a falling carbon dioxide partial pressure on the ratio

options.text: Both values changed in the same proportion, so their ratio was unchanged and the pH held
options.misconception: claims a constant ratio where the note shows the ratio falling from twenty to nine

questions.explanation: The resting pair gives a ratio of 24 over 1.2, which is twenty, and the exercising pair gives 14 over 1.5, which is about nine and a third, so the ratio fell by more than half and the pH fell with it. During hard exercise the working muscle adds hydrogen ions, which the bicarbonate absorbs by becoming carbon dioxide and water, so the bicarbonate is used up while the carbon dioxide partial pressure rises, and the buffer's reserve is exactly what is being spent. The tempting belief that more bicarbonate means a lower pH fails because raising bicarbonate raises the ratio and the pH. The belief that a falling carbon dioxide partial pressure lowers the pH fails because it enlarges the ratio. The belief that the ratio held fails because the note's own numbers give twenty against nine.
questions.hint: Compute the ratio in each sample before deciding which of the two values did the work.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why a Low pH Favours Unloading
questions.learningObjective: explain the pH dependence of oxygen unloading from a binding model

stimulus.body: Haemoglobin note (written for this course): Oxygen binding is described here by an expression in which the fraction of sites filled equals the oxygen partial pressure raised to the power 2.8, divided by that quantity plus the half-saturation pressure raised to the power 2.8, where the half-saturation pressure is the partial pressure at which the fraction filled is one half. For arterial blood the half-saturation pressure is 26 millimetres of mercury. For tissue at a lower pH it is 32. Working through the expression at a tissue partial pressure of 40 gives a fraction filled of 0.77 in the arterial case and 0.65 in the low-pH case, and at a partial pressure of 100 the two cases give 0.98 and 0.96.

questions.stem: Using only the haemoglobin note, why does the tissue take up more oxygen in the low-pH case?

options.text: The lower pH raises the half-saturation pressure, so the same partial pressure leaves fewer sites filled
The lower pH lowers the half-saturation pressure, so the same partial pressure fills more sites
options.misconception: reverses the effect of the low pH on the half-saturation pressure

options.text: The lower pH changes the power of 2.8, so the same partial pressure now fills every site at once
options.misconception: moves the effect to the exponent and leaves the half-saturation pressure unchanged

options.text: The lower pH has no effect on filling, since only the partial pressure can alter the fraction
options.misconception: denies the shift that the note reports between the two sets of numbers

questions.explanation: Raising the half-saturation pressure shifts the whole relationship to the right, so at any given partial pressure fewer sites are occupied, and the note's own figures show the fraction filled falling from 0.77 to 0.65 while the arterial figure barely moves. That is the mechanism behind the effect of carbon dioxide and hydrogen ions on haemoglobin, and it works in the tissues' favour: the place that needs the oxygen is the place where oxygen is released most readily. The tempting belief that the shift runs the other way fails because the note's half-saturation pressure rises from 26 to 32. The belief that the exponent changes fails because it is the same 2.8 in both cases. The belief that only the partial pressure matters fails because the note shows a difference at the same partial pressure.
questions.hint: Compare the two fillings at the same partial pressure and see which parameter moved.

questions.topic: Physiology: Comparing the Reach of Two Signal Types
questions.learningObjective: use concentration data to contrast the reach of a hormone and a neurotransmitter

stimulus.body: Distribution note (written for this course): Two signal molecules are followed from the moment they are released. Molecule one is released from a gland directly into the blood at 20 nanograms per millilitre. A sample taken at the gland reads 20, a sample from a capillary bed in the target organ reads 18, and a sample from a vein further along the same vessel still reads 18. Molecule two is released from a nerve ending into a narrow gap between two cells, and the samples read 20 at the ending, 12 on the far side of the gap, and 0.6 in blood drawn from the same region of the body ten millimetres away.

questions.stem: Using only the distribution note, which comparison between the two molecules does the data support?

One is destroyed by the blood, the other survives indefinitely in the narrow gap between cells

options.misconception: claims both reach everywhere when one is measured falling away within millimetres

options.text: Both stay near their source, and the two sets of readings simply reflect different release doses
options.misconception: dismisses the readings as different doses when the release point reads twenty for both

The belief that both reach everywhere fails because the second is measured to be almost absent a few millimetres out. The belief that the readings are just different doses fails because both start at the same twenty at release.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Identifying the Response in a Temperature Trace
questions.learningObjective: separate the response from the set point and the outcome in a control loop

stimulus.body: Field note (written for this course): A person rests in a room held at 30 degrees Celsius. Core temperature and skin temperature are logged every fifteen minutes, and the sweating rate is rated. At minute 0 the core reads 37.0, the skin 33, and the sweating rate is low. At minute 15 the core reads 37.2, the skin 34, and the sweating rate is high. At minute 30 the core reads 37.1, the skin 33.5, and the sweating rate is moderate. At minute 45 the core reads 37.0, the skin 33, and the sweating rate is low again. The room temperature is unchanged throughout.

questions.stem: Using only the field note, which entry in the record is the response that opposes the disturbance?

options.text: The skin warming and the sweating rise over the first fifteen minutes, which together increase heat loss
The return of the core reading to 37.0 at minute 45, which is what caused the earlier rise
options.misconception: reverses cause and effect by making the recovery the cause of the disturbance

options.text: The room temperature held at 30 degrees, which is the controlled variable that is being defended
options.misconception: mistakes the environmental disturbance for the thing the loop is correcting

options.text: The fall in sweating after minute 30, which produced the rise in core temperature earlier
options.misconception: treats a later reduction in cooling as the cause of an earlier warming

questions.explanation: In a control loop the response is the part that acts to oppose the disturbance, and here the sweat rate and the skin temperature both climb while the core temperature is high, which is exactly the signature of a body shedding heat: more evaporation and more blood flow near the surface. As the core reading falls back, both responses fall away too, which is what a negative loop looks like. The tempting belief that the recovery caused the rise fails because it came after the rise. The belief that the room temperature is the controlled variable fails because the room is the disturbance, held still so the loop's work is visible. The belief that the later fall in sweating caused the earlier rise fails because it followed the rise rather than preceding it.
questions.hint: Ask which measured quantity moved in the direction that would reduce the disturbance.

questions.learningObjective: compute alveolar ventilation from tidal volume, rate and dead space

stimulus.body: Ventilation note (written for this course): A person breathing quietly has a tidal volume of 500 millilitres at 12 breaths per minute. Measured at the mouth, 150 millilitres of each 500 fills the conducting airways and comes back out unchanged, so it never takes part in gas exchange. The same person then breathes more deeply at 20 breaths per minute with the tidal volume unchanged at 500 millilitres, and the 150 millilitres of airway volume is repeated at every breath.

questions.stem: Using only the ventilation note, how does the volume of air reaching the gas-exchanging surfaces change?

options.text: It rises from 4,200 to 7,000 millilitres per minute, because airway volume is repeated at every breath
It stays at 4,200 millilitres per minute, because the airway volume is filled whatever the rate
options.misconception: believes a faster rate adds nothing once the airway volume is subtracted once

options.text: It rises from 5,100 to 9,100 millilitres per minute, because only part of each breath is airway
options.misconception: counts the airway volume once for the whole minute instead of once for each breath

options.text: It falls, because each deeper breath traps a larger share of its volume in the conducting airways
options.misconception: believes a deeper breath increases the wasted share of the volume inspired

questions.explanation: The volume reaching the alveoli is the tidal volume less the airway volume, multiplied by the breathing rate, and the airway volume has to be subtracted at every breath because every breath fills it again. At 12 breaths the figure is 350 times 12, which is 4,200, and at 20 breaths it is 350 times 20, which is 7,000. The tempting belief that the value cannot change fails because the 350 figure is per breath and more breaths deliver more usable air. The belief that the airway volume is subtracted once per minute fails because it is refilled on every single breath, and that is the error producing the 5,100 and 9,100 figures. The belief that deeper breaths waste more fails because the airway volume is a fixed volume rather than a fraction of the breath.
questions.hint: Work out the usable volume of one breath, then multiply by the number of breaths.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Testing a Resting Potential Against Two Equilibrium Values
questions.learningObjective: use the equilibrium relation to explain a measured resting potential

stimulus.body: Electrochemical note (written for this course): For an ion at 37 degrees Celsius, the equilibrium potential in millivolts is 61.5 times the logarithm to base ten of the outside concentration divided by the inside concentration. The concentrations measured in a cell, all in millimoles per litre, are potassium 5 outside and 140 inside, and sodium 145 outside and 12 inside. Working through the relation gives about minus 89 millivolts for potassium and about plus 67 millivolts for sodium. The voltage actually recorded across the resting membrane is about minus 70.

questions.stem: Using only the electrochemical note, which single calculation best explains the recorded resting potential?

options.text: The value lies between the two, but much nearer the potassium one because that ion dominates at rest
The value lies between the two, but much nearer the sodium one because that ion dominates at rest
options.misconception: puts the value near the wrong ion and reverses which permeability is larger

options.text: Both ions give about minus seventy on their own, so the measured value needs no explanation
options.misconception: believes each ion independently predicts the recorded resting value

options.text: The value sits at the midpoint of the two, because the membrane weights both ions equally at rest
options.misconception: assumes equal weighting, which would put the value close to minus eleven instead

questions.explanation: The recorded value sits about 19 millivolts from the potassium figure and about 137 from the sodium one, so the membrane is dominated by potassium even though the two equilibrium values are about 156 millivolts apart. That dominance is a statement about permeability, because the resting membrane passes potassium far more readily than sodium, and the small sodium leak keeps the value short of the potassium figure. The tempting belief that sodium dominates fails because a value pinned near plus 67 would not be negative at all. The belief that each ion predicts the recorded value fails because neither one does on its own. The belief that the two are weighted equally fails because an equal weighting would put the reading near the middle of the two, which is nowhere near minus seventy.
questions.hint: Measure the distance from the recorded value to each of the two figures.

questions.topic: Physiology: Which Sample Would Gain Most from Faster Breathing
questions.learningObjective: compare pH responses to a fall in carbon dioxide while bicarbonate is held fixed

stimulus.body: Buffer note (written for this course): Four blood samples are reported with a bicarbonate concentration, a carbon dioxide partial pressure and a pH, checked with the relation that pH equals 6.1 plus the logarithm of bicarbonate divided by 0.03 times the carbon dioxide partial pressure. Sample one: bicarbonate 24, carbon dioxide 40, pH 7.40. Sample two: bicarbonate 14, carbon dioxide 30, pH 7.29. Sample three: bicarbonate 30, carbon dioxide 30, pH 7.62. Sample four: bicarbonate 20, carbon dioxide 50, pH 7.23. Each sample is now imagined with its carbon dioxide lowered to 30 and its bicarbonate left exactly as it is.

questions.stem: Using only the buffer note, which sample's pH would rise the most when its carbon dioxide is lowered to 30?

options.text: Sample four, because the same fall in carbon dioxide enlarges its smaller ratio by the most
Sample one, because it has the largest bicarbonate and so the most to gain from the change
options.misconception: believes the largest bicarbonate gives the biggest pH rise and ignores the ratio

options.text: Sample three, because it has the highest starting pH and so has the furthest room to rise
options.misconception: picks the highest starting pH although that sample cannot change at all

options.text: Sample two, because a bicarbonate that low means the ratio is already close to its final value
options.misconception: thinks the lowest bicarbonate sits nearest the new ratio, when it sits furthest off

questions.explanation: The pH follows the ratio rather than either value on its own, so a given fall in dissolved carbon dioxide moves the pH most where the ratio was smallest. Working the note through: sample one moves from a ratio of 20 to 26.7, sample two is already at 30 so it does not move, sample three is already at 30 so it does not move, and sample four moves from 13.3 to 22.2, which is the largest change of the three that move, worth about 0.22 of a pH unit against 0.13 for sample one. The tempting belief that the largest bicarbonate wins fails because a larger bicarbonate also means a larger ratio to begin with. The belief that the highest starting pH wins fails because samples two and three do not change at all. The belief about a low bicarbonate being near its final value fails because it is furthest from the new value.
questions.hint: Convert each sample to a ratio before and after, then compare the changes.
