questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Reading a Conductance Trace Through One Impulse
questions.learningObjective: infer the timing of sodium inactivation from a conductance trace

stimulus.body: Conductance note (written for this course): A membrane is impaled and the sodium and potassium conductances are followed through one action potential, each expressed as a fraction of its own peak value. At the resting point both read 0.02. Ten milliseconds after the stimulus the sodium conductance reads 1.00 while the potassium conductance reads 0.10. At thirty milliseconds the sodium conductance reads 0.15 while the potassium conductance reads 1.00. Ninety milliseconds after the peak both conductances read 0.05 and the voltage has returned to its resting value.

questions.stem: Using only the conductance note, what accounts for the sodium conductance falling during the spike?

options.text: The sodium channels open first and then inactivate, so the inward current stops while potassium continues
The sodium channels close because the potassium conductance has become the larger of the two
options.misconception: makes a channel property depend on a different channel's conductance

options.text: The sodium ions leave the cell as soon as the channels open, which reverses the sodium current
options.misconception: turns a channel behaviour into an ion movement that the trace does not show

options.text: The channels are removed from the membrane and rebuilt later, which accounts for the delay
options.misconception: replaces a change in an existing channel with the removal and rebuilding of channels

questions.explanation: The trace shows the two conductances taking turns rather than rising together, and the only reading that fits a channel property is that the sodium channels open quickly and then inactivate, staying closed for the rest of the spike even while the voltage is still high. The potassium channels open later and more slowly, which is why the outward current and the recovery come after the peak. The tempting belief that the sodium channels are shut by the rising potassium fails because a channel's inactivation is timed by its own voltage sensing, not by a neighbour. The belief that sodium reverses direction fails because the driving force only reverses after the voltage crosses zero, and the trace shows conductance, not flow. The belief that channels are removed fails because removal and rebuilding would take far longer than the tens of milliseconds recorded.
questions.hint: Ask whether the fall is a property of the channel itself or of something happening to the ions.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Separating the Electrical and Calcium Events in a Contraction
questions.learningObjective: use timing and a blocking drug to identify the steps of excitation-contraction coupling

stimulus.body: Muscle note (written for this course): A single muscle fibre is impaled and the free calcium inside it is followed through one contraction. At rest the reading is 90 nanomoles per litre. When a stimulus arrives the reading rises to 400 within 20 milliseconds and then falls back to 90 over the next 200. The depolarisation recorded at the surface of the same fibre lasts only 2 milliseconds. A second fibre is treated with a drug that leaves the electrical recording unchanged but prevents the sarcoplasmic reticulum from releasing calcium, and its calcium reading never leaves 90 while the recorded depolarisation is normal.

questions.stem: Using only the muscle note, which statement about excitation-contraction coupling is supported?

options.text: The electrical event is over long before the calcium rise, and the rise is required for the tension
The electrical event and the calcium rise are one event lasting the whole two hundred milliseconds
options.misconception: collapses two separately timed events into a single long one

options.text: The calcium rise is caused by calcium entering the fibre from outside through the surface membrane
options.misconception: credits the outside rather than the internal store, which the drug shows is essential

options.text: The drug raised the resting calcium to 400, so the contraction was protected rather than blocked
options.misconception: reverses what a blocking drug did to a reading and invents a higher resting value

questions.explanation: The timings separate the two events cleanly: the depolarisation is over in 2 milliseconds while the calcium rise lasts about 200, so the calcium change cannot be the depolarisation itself and must be the consequence of it. The drug then identifies which step is essential, because blocking the internal release leaves the electrical event intact and the calcium flat, which means the surface event is neither necessary nor sufficient on its own and the internal store sits between the two. The tempting belief that the events are one fails because the note measures them separately and they differ by two orders of magnitude in duration. The belief about calcium entering from outside fails because the drug blocks the response without touching the electrical event, and the internal store is what is being emptied.
questions.hint: Compare the two durations first, then use the drug to see which step the tension depends on.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Reading a Four-Cell Diffusion Comparison
questions.learningObjective: read a controlled series of membrane preparations and state the governing relation

stimulus.body: Diffusion note (written for this course): A single membrane sheet of a fixed substance is cut into pieces and set up in four diffusion cells. Cell one has an area of 10 square centimetres and a thickness of 2 micrometres. Cell two is the same substance with its area doubled to 20 square centimetres. Cell three is the same substance with its thickness doubled to 4 micrometres. Cell four has both area and thickness doubled, to 20 square centimetres and 4 micrometres. The recorded rate of passage is 5 units per minute in cell one, 10 in cell two, 2.5 in cell three, and 1.25 in cell four.

questions.stem: Using only the diffusion note, which relation does the four-cell series illustrate?

options.text: The rate rises with area and falls with thickness, so the two changes act in opposite directions
The rate rises with both area and thickness, so a thicker sheet passes more per minute
options.misconception: believes thickness adds to the rate instead of opposing it

options.text: The rate depends on area alone, so the thickest cell should pass as much as the widest
options.misconception: believes thickness has no effect and leaves cell three unexplained

options.text: The rate depends on thickness alone, so the widest cell should pass as little as the thinnest
options.misconception: believes area has no effect and leaves cell two unexplained

questions.explanation: The four cells hold everything constant except area and thickness, so the differences isolate their effects: doubling the area doubles the rate because twice as much membrane is available, doubling the thickness quarters nothing but halves the rate because each molecule has twice as far to diffuse, and doing both gives a rate a quarter of the original. The series is the experimental form of the relation that the rate is proportional to area and to the inverse of thickness. The tempting belief that thickness helps fails because thickness is the distance a molecule must cross, not a quantity of membrane. The belief that area is the only factor fails because cell three halves the rate with its area unchanged, and the belief that thickness is the only factor fails because cell two doubles the rate with its thickness unchanged.
questions.hint: Cell four changed two things at once, so use it to check cells two and three against each other.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Separating Reabsorption From Dilution in the Urine
questions.learningObjective: use two urine concentrations to show that a solute is neither reabsorbed nor secreted

stimulus.body: Renal note (written for this course): A solute is filtered at 125 millilitres per minute and is not a substance the tubule handles specially. Its concentration in plasma is 2 milligrams per millilitre, so 250 milligrams of it are filtered every minute. Urine leaves at 1 millilitre per minute. In a first collection the solute in the urine reads 250 milligrams per millilitre. A drug is then given that doubles the urine flow to 2 millilitres per minute while the filtration rate and the plasma concentration are unchanged, and the solute in the urine now reads 125 milligrams per millilitre.

questions.stem: Using only the renal note, what does the second reading show about how the tubule handled the solute?

options.text: It was neither reabsorbed nor secreted, because the same filtered mass is now spread over twice the volume
It was reabsorbed, because the same filtered mass now appears in a larger and therefore stronger volume
options.misconception: reads a halving of concentration as evidence that something was taken back

options.text: It was secreted, because the concentration fell even though the mass filtered each minute was unchanged
options.misconception: calls a fall in concentration an addition of solute to the tubule

options.text: It was partly reabsorbed, because a rise in flow should otherwise have raised the concentration
options.misconception: expects a flow rise to concentrate the urine, which is the opposite of what happens

questions.explanation: The filtered mass is fixed at 250 milligrams a minute by the filtration rate and the plasma concentration, and both were held constant, so the same mass leaves in both collections. It appears at 250 milligrams per millilitre in one and 125 in the other, and that is exactly the halving you get from doubling the volume with the mass unchanged, so no transport step took place and the concentration moved only because the water did. The tempting belief that this shows reabsorption fails because reabsorption would remove mass and make the concentration rise rather than fall. The belief that it shows secretion fails because secretion would add mass and raise the concentration. The belief about a flow rise concentrating the urine fails because more water leaving dilutes whatever is in the tubule.
questions.hint: Fix the mass filtered each minute, then ask whether the change in concentration needs any transport at all.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Design a Test That a Voltage Depends on Ion Gradients
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test that a resting voltage responds to the ion distribution
questions.stem: A student claims that a cell's resting voltage is fixed and does not depend on the surrounding solution. Describe an experiment that would test the claim, and name two things that must be held the same in every preparation for the test to be fair.

answer.exemplar: Place identical cells into a series of bathing solutions that differ in one ion at a time, keeping the concentration of every other ion the same, and record the voltage across the membrane in each. A series that changes potassium alone, and a parallel series that changes sodium alone, together show whether the voltage responds to either distribution rather than being constant by construction. The same cells, the same temperature, the same pH and the same waiting time before each reading must be held constant, and the series must be run in a random order, because a voltage that simply drifted over the course of the experiment could otherwise be mistaken for an ion effect. The essential comparison is between solutions that differ in one ion only: if the voltage moves when potassium is changed and does not move when an unrelated ion is changed by the same amount, the claim that the voltage is fixed cannot be sustained, and if the voltage never moves at all then something in the preparation is holding it constant and the test has not probed what it was meant to.

questions.explanation: The design has to change the suspected cause and nothing else, which is why the series varies one ion at a time and holds temperature, pH and cell type fixed. Without a control ion varied by the same amount, a general damage effect from changing the solution would be indistinguishable from a specific gradient effect.
questions.hint: Ask what else besides the one ion would change when you change its concentration.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Design a Test for Carrier-Mediated Transport
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test that a transported solute uses saturable carriers
questions.stem: A solute is claimed to cross a membrane through carrier proteins rather than dissolving through the lipid. Describe an experiment that would test the claim, and say what result would count against it.

answer.exemplar: Expose identical cells to a series of outside concentrations of the solute, spanning a range wide enough that any ceiling on the rate should appear, and measure the initial rate of transport into the cells at each concentration. Then repeat the series with a second compound known to use the same carrier present alongside the first. If carriers are doing the work, the rate will rise steeply at first and then level off at a ceiling, because every carrier is occupied, and adding the second compound will depress that ceiling at every concentration because the two compete for the same proteins. If instead the rate keeps rising in direct proportion to the concentration with no ceiling, the claim is not supported, because a simple lipid route behaves that way. Temperature, cell number, pH and the time over which the initial rate is measured must be held the same across the series, and the concentration order should be varied so that a drifting preparation is not mistaken for saturation.

questions.explanation: A carrier is defined by its capacity, so the discriminating measurement is the shape of the rate against concentration curve rather than the speed of transport. The competition arm matters because it separates a carrier from a channel that simply lets more solute through, and a preparation that drifts over the course of a long series would produce a false ceiling.
questions.hint: Ask what a limited number of proteins would have to do to the rate as the concentration rises.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Design a Test That Localises a Drug's Action at a Synapse
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test that distinguishes a drug acting on the receptor from one acting on transmitter breakdown
questions.stem: A drug prolongs the response of a nerve to a stimulus, and it is not known whether the drug blocks the receptor on the receiving membrane or slows the enzyme that breaks the transmitter down in the gap. Describe an experiment that would separate those two possibilities.

answer.exemplar: Apply the drug to two preparations that differ in where the synapse sits relative to the drug. In one, the drug is present only on the receiving side, so the transmitter is still broken down normally and only the receptor is exposed; in the other, the drug is applied only on the sending side and the receiving membrane is untouched, which changes the rate at which transmitter is released without touching either receptor or enzyme. Alongside both, measure three things for every stimulus: the size of the potential in the receiving cell, the time that potential lasts, and how much transmitter is present in the gap. A drug that blocks the receptor lowers the size of the response and shortens nothing, because the transmitter is still cleared on time, while a drug that slows breakdown leaves the size unchanged and stretches the duration, with the gap measurement showing more transmitter present for longer. If the effect appears at a distance from the site of application, that argues against a purely local block and points to something circulating.

questions.explanation: The two mechanisms differ in whether the size of the response or its duration changes, so the experiment has to record both rather than either alone. Applying the drug to one side of the synapse only also rules out an action somewhere else entirely, such as a change in how much transmitter is released.
questions.hint: Ask which measurement would change under one mechanism and stay the same under the other.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Design a Test That a Drug Acts on the Medullary Gradient
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test of whether a drug changes the kidney's medullary solute gradient
questions.stem: A drug increases the volume of urine produced. It is not known whether the drug works by blocking the transport of solute out of the loop, by blocking water reabsorption in the duct, or by changing how much water is filtered at all. Describe an experiment that would separate those three possibilities.

answer.exemplar: Measure three quantities in the same animals, before and after the drug, and read them against an untreated control group given a placebo. First, the concentration of the fluid leaving the collecting duct, which separates a duct-level block from the other two: a duct that cannot reabsorb water leaves the fluid dilute whatever happens further upstream, whereas a blocked loop leaves the interstitium unable to become concentrated in the first place. Second, the osmolarity of the interstitium at the tip of the medulla, sampled directly, which is high when the loop is pumping solute out and falls toward that of plasma when the loop is blocked. Third, the filtration rate, measured by a solute that is filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, which distinguishes a change in how much is filtered from a change in what is done with it afterwards. Comparing the three readings against the control separates the three sites, and sampling the medulla directly is what stops a fall in urine concentration being mistaken for a failure of the gradient.

questions.explanation: The three candidate sites sit at different points in the pathway, so each needs its own reading rather than a single measurement of urine volume. Measuring the medulla directly is the part that distinguishes a loop that is not concentrating from a duct that cannot reabsorb, because both can give a dilute urine.
questions.hint: Ask what you would have to measure inside the kidney to tell a loop problem from a duct problem.

questions.topic: Physiology: Design a Test That a Response Is a Negative Feedback Loop
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test that a physiological response opposes its disturbance
questions.stem: A student claims that shivering after a drop in temperature is a positive feedback loop because the body is making the disturbance worse. Describe an experiment that would test whether the response opposes or amplifies the disturbance, and say what observation would support the claim.

answer.exemplar: Perturb a group of people in a controlled way, by placing them in a cold room at a known temperature for a known time, and log the core temperature and the shivering rate every few minutes throughout. Run a comparison group kept comfortably warm, and a third group perturbed in the opposite direction, by a warm room, so that the response is seen in both signs. If the response is a negative loop, then the cold group's temperature falls and then climbs back towards its starting value while the shivering rate rises and then falls again, and the warm group's temperature behaves the mirror image, with the rate of heat loss rising rather than falling. A single unperturbed group is not enough, because a response that simply tracks the disturbance would look identical in one direction. Reading the rates rather than the temperature alone matters, because the temperature is the thing being corrected and the rate is the loop's output, and a genuine negative loop shows the output rising as the error grows and fading as the error closes.

questions.explanation: Testing one direction only cannot tell a correcting response from a merely correlated one, so the design needs the mirrored perturbation and an unperturbed control. Watching the rate of the response rise and then fade, in step with the size of the error, is what identifies the sign of the loop.
questions.hint: Ask what a comparison in the opposite direction of perturbation would show.

questions.topic: Physiology: Design a Test That Folding Raises Absorptive Surface
questions.learningObjective: design a controlled test of the effect of folding on absorption rate
questions.stem: Absorptive tissue is thrown into folds that carry projections rather than being left flat. Describe an experiment that would test whether the folding raises the rate at which a nutrient is absorbed, and name one way the test could give a misleading answer.

answer.exemplar: Take two matched pieces of the same tissue, one left flat and one folded, cut to the same mass and the same surface volume, place each in the same solution at the same concentration and temperature, and measure how fast the nutrient disappears from the solution or appears in the tissue over the first few minutes. Repeat with several pieces of each rather than one, since a single piece gives no sense of the spread. The result that supports the claim is a faster uptake into the folded piece even though its mass and its solution are identical, which can only be explained by more surface being presented. A misleading answer would come from the folds trapping unstirred solution in their crevices, so a transport-limited reading could be measuring how well the flask was shaken rather than how much surface was offered; stirring both chambers at the same rate, and washing the folded piece so liquid trapped in the folds is counted, removes that alternative. Measuring over the first minutes also matters, because later the tissue runs out of nutrient and the curves converge regardless of surface area.

questions.explanation: The two pieces must be matched in everything except folding, and the early rate is the measurement that isolates surface from supply. Stirring crevice liquid is the confound that most easily produces a false positive, because trapped solution makes the folded piece look better supplied than it is.
questions.hint: Ask what else a folded surface does besides presenting more area.

options.text: Four times, then twelve times, so the duct is concentrating the fluid again
Four times, then four times, so the second figure only restates the first comparison
options.misconception: measures the final urine against plasma again instead of against the limb fluid

options.text: Twelve times, then four times, so the two comparisons have been put in the wrong order
options.misconception: swaps which value is divided by which and reports the pair back to front

options.text: Four times, then six times, so the second figure divides by the wrong earlier value
options.misconception: divides the tip value by the descending limb fluid rather than the ascending one

questions.explanation: Twelve hundred divided by three hundred is four, so the medulla at its tip is four times as concentrated as the plasma it came from, which is what makes pulling water out of the duct possible at all. The ascending limb leaves the fluid at a hundred, and the final urine at twelve hundred is twelve times that, so the second twelve-fold gain is done by water leaving the fluid in the collecting duct rather than by solute being added. The tempting belief that the second figure repeats the first fails because it divides by a different quantity. The belief that the order is reversed fails because the question fixes which value is compared with which. The belief about six fails because six is what the tip figure is divided by when the descending limb value of six hundred is used instead of the ascending limb value.
questions.hint: Divide the tip value by the plasma, then divide the final urine by the value leaving the ascending limb.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Computing Oxygen Consumption From Flow and Content
questions.learningObjective: compute oxygen consumption from cardiac output and the arterial to venous difference
questions.stem: Oxygen consumption is calculated as the cardiac output in decilitres per minute multiplied by the difference in oxygen content between arterial and venous blood in millilitres per decilitre. At rest the cardiac output is 5 litres per minute, the arterial content is 20 and the venous 15. At maximum effort the cardiac output is 35 litres per minute and the venous content is 4, with the arterial content unchanged. First work out the consumption at rest, then the consumption at maximum effort, both in millilitres per minute.

options.text: 250 at rest, then 5,600 at maximum effort, which is about twenty-two times the rest value
250 at rest, then 1,750 at maximum effort, which scales by the change in flow alone
options.misconception: scales the rest value by the flow increase and ignores the wider extraction

options.text: 1,000 at rest, then 7,000 at maximum effort, which treats all arterial content as extracted
options.misconception: counts the whole arterial content instead of the part that leaves the tissue

options.text: 250 at rest, then 1,400 at maximum effort, which counts only the venous content
options.misconception: multiplies the flow by the venous content rather than by the difference

questions.explanation: At rest the flow is 50 decilitres a minute and the difference is 5, so consumption is 250. At maximum effort the flow is 350 and the difference has widened to 16, so consumption is 5,600, about twenty-two times the resting figure. The rise is not all flow: the flow rises sevenfold while extraction rises a little over threefold, and together they account for the increase. The tempting belief that only flow matters fails because it would give 1,750 and would leave the widening difference unexplained. The belief that all arterial content is used fails because that would mean the venous blood carried no oxygen at all. The belief that the venous content is the difference fails because the difference is the two subtracted, not either one alone.
questions.hint: Convert the cardiac output to decilitres first, and subtract the venous content from the arterial one.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Backing a Bicarbonate Concentration Out of a pH
questions.learningObjective: invert a buffer relation and compare the result with a resting value
questions.stem: A blood sample is measured at a pH of 7.50 while the carbon dioxide partial pressure is 25 millimetres of mercury. The relation used is that pH equals 6.1 plus the logarithm of the bicarbonate concentration divided by 0.03 times the carbon dioxide partial pressure, and a usual resting bicarbonate concentration is 24 millimoles per litre. First work out the bicarbonate concentration implied by the measured pH, then state how it compares with that resting value.

options.text: About 18.8 millimoles per litre, which is roughly 5 below the resting value of 24
About 25.1 millimoles per litre, which is just above the resting value of 24
options.misconception: reports the logarithm before multiplying by the dissolved carbon dioxide term

options.text: About 18.8 millimoles per litre, which is roughly 5 above the resting value of 24
options.misconception: computes the concentration correctly and then reverses the direction of the comparison

options.text: About 24 millimoles per litre, which is exactly the resting value once it has been rounded
options.misconception: assumes the concentration is unchanged and ignores the measured pH entirely

questions.explanation: Turning the relation round, the ratio of bicarbonate to dissolved carbon dioxide is ten to the power of 0.4, which is about 25, and the dissolved carbon dioxide is 0.03 times 25, which is 0.75, so the bicarbonate is about 25 times 0.75, or 18.8. That is roughly 5 below the resting 24, and the reason is visible in the ratio: removing carbon dioxide by breathing faster shrinks the denominator, and with the bicarbonate also consumed by buffering hydrogen ions the concentration falls rather than holding. The tempting belief that the logarithm alone is the answer fails because it is a ratio and still has to be scaled by the carbon dioxide. The belief that the comparison is reversed fails because 18.8 is smaller than 24. The belief that the value is unchanged fails because a pH of 7.50 with a carbon dioxide of 25 cannot sit on a ratio of 20.
questions.hint: Raise ten to the power of the pH difference, then multiply by the dissolved carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Measuring How Much of a Rise a Loop Has Corrected
questions.learningObjective: compute a rise above a baseline and the fraction of it that has been corrected
questions.stem: A person who has not eaten for twelve hours has a blood glucose of 5.0 units per litre. Two hours after a large meal the reading is at its highest at 7.5, and four hours after the meal it has fallen to 5.5. First work out how far the peak rose above the fasting level, then state what fraction of that rise has been removed by the four-hour reading.

options.text: A rise of 2.5 units, with four fifths of it removed and 0.5 still above fasting
A rise of 2.5 units, with only one fifth of it removed and 2.0 still above fasting
options.misconception: inverts the removed and remaining parts of the rise

options.text: A rise of 0.5 units, with four fifths of it removed and 0.1 still above fasting
options.misconception: measures the part still remaining and calls that the original rise

options.text: A rise of 2.5 units, with none of it removed and the whole 2.5 still above fasting
options.misconception: ignores the falling reading between the peak and the four-hour sample

questions.explanation: The peak stood 2.5 above the fasting level, and at four hours the reading is 0.5 above it, so 2.0 of the original 2.5 has gone, which is four fifths. What makes the pattern evidence of a restoring loop is that the correction tracks the size of the deviation: the larger the excess above the fasting level, the more hormone is released to remove glucose, and as the excess shrinks the response fades with it. The tempting belief that only one fifth was removed fails because 2.0 and 0.5 have been swapped. The belief that the rise was 0.5 fails because that is the remainder at four hours rather than the peak excursion. The belief that nothing was removed fails because the four-hour reading is lower than the peak, which is the whole observation.
questions.hint: Measure the peak against the fasting value, then measure the four-hour value against the same baseline.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why the Resting Voltage Is Nobody's Single Value
questions.learningObjective: explain why a resting voltage is a net result rather than one ion's equilibrium value
questions.stem: A measured resting voltage of about minus 70 millivolts matches neither the value potassium alone would give nor the value sodium alone would give. Explain why the resting voltage is a net figure rather than any one ion's, and say which ion has the greater influence on it.

answer.exemplar: Each ion on its own would pull the membrane towards the voltage at which its own chemical and electrical gradients balance, and those voltages are far apart: with the concentrations given, potassium alone would sit near minus 89 and sodium alone near plus 67, a gap of about 156 millivolts. The real membrane does not reach either, because at rest it is permeable to both ions, so both are pulling at once and the value that results is a weighted compromise between them. The weighting is set by how easily each ion gets through, and the resting membrane passes potassium far more readily than sodium, so the compromise lies most of the way towards the potassium figure while the small sodium leak keeps it short of it. Numerically the measured minus 70 is about 19 millivolts from the potassium value and about 137 from the sodium one, which is the arithmetic statement of the same point. The tempting belief that the resting voltage equals the potassium figure fails because that would require the membrane to be completely impermeable to sodium, and it is not. The belief that the two ions average equally fails because an equal weighting would put the voltage near the middle of the two figures, close to minus 11, which is nothing like the measured value.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to establish that two separate gradients are acting at once and that the relative permeabilities decide the weighting, because that is what makes the value a compromise rather than a copy of either ion's prediction.
questions.hint: Ask which ion the measured value is closer to, and what would make it closer.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why Working Tissue Unloads More Oxygen
questions.learningObjective: explain the chain from working tissue to haemoglobin releasing more oxygen
questions.stem: In a working muscle the pH falls and the carbon dioxide partial pressure rises. Explain, step by step, why that makes haemoglobin give up more oxygen at exactly the place that is using it.

answer.exemplar: The chain runs from the muscle's own chemistry to the shape of the haemoglobin. A working muscle produces carbon dioxide, and it also produces hydrogen ions, both of which accumulate in the tissue fluid as the muscle works, which is why the pH falls. The falling pH and the rising carbon dioxide both act on haemoglobin to reduce its affinity for oxygen: the half-saturation pressure rises, so the same oxygen partial pressure leaves fewer of the binding sites occupied, and the curve is said to shift to the right. Because the tissue fluid is also the place where the partial pressure of oxygen is lowest, the two effects push in the same direction, and haemoglobin unloads more rather than less in exactly the tissue that is consuming oxygen. The reverse happens in the lungs, where oxygenation of the blood reduces the hydrogen ion and carbon dioxide load and raises the affinity again, so haemoglobin reloads. The tempting belief that the effect works through the partial pressure fails because the partial pressure of oxygen falls in the tissue anyway, and the affinity change adds to that rather than replacing it. The belief that carbon dioxide competes directly for binding sites fails because the dominant route is through the change in hydrogen ions and the resulting change in the shape of the protein.

questions.explanation: The explanation must show that the affinity change and the partial pressure fall combine, since the mechanism only makes sense if the tissue is both the place with the least oxygen and the place where affinity is lowest.
questions.hint: Ask what the working tissue does to two things at once, and where both of them are lowest.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Why a Short Gut Can Absorb So Much
questions.learningObjective: explain how structure, blood supply and drainage together raise absorption
questions.stem: The small intestine is only a few metres long yet takes up nearly all of the digested nutrients from a meal. Explain how its structure, the way digestion finishes there, and the way the absorbed material is carried away all contribute to that capacity.

answer.exemplar: Three separate features add up, and none of them is the length of the gut. First the lining is thrown into circular folds, each fold carrying villi, and each villus covered in a brush border of microvilli, so the area available is multiplied at three nested scales rather than being the area of a smooth tube. Second the gut is where digestion is finished rather than started, because pancreatic juice and bile are delivered here, so the material arriving is already broken to units small enough to cross a membrane at all; a nutrient that is still locked inside a large molecule cannot be absorbed no matter how much surface is presented. Third the absorbed material is removed quickly rather than accumulating, with blood capillaries carrying water-soluble nutrients away to keep the concentration difference across the lining steep, and the lymph carrying absorbed fat away, which is what preserves the gradient that passive movement needs. Steady mixing by the wall movements and the short path from lumen to capillary also keeps the layer next to the lining thin. The tempting belief that length alone explains it fails because a smooth tube of that length would present a small fraction of the area. The belief that surface area is sufficient fails because digestion has to be complete before anything can cross. The belief that removal is unimportant fails because absorption is driven by a gradient that a stagnant layer would abolish.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to show that area, completeness of digestion and removal of what is absorbed are three separate contributions, because the common wrong answer treats surface area as the only one of them.
questions.hint: Ask what would limit absorption if the surface were large but the gradient across the lining were lost.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: What a Limiting Factor Does to a Response
questions.learningObjective: explain why a response is capped by whichever factor reaches its own limit first
questions.stem: A trained athlete can increase oxygen consumption about twenty-fold above the resting value. Explain why that figure is a ceiling set by the system rather than a property of the muscles alone, and describe what would happen if only one of the two factors involved were improved.

answer.exemplar: The muscles are capable of consuming far more oxygen than the body can supply, so the ceiling belongs to the supply side. Consumption is the product of two things: how much blood reaches the tissue each minute, and how much oxygen each unit of that blood gives up as it passes. At rest the flow is about 5 litres a minute and the arterial to venous difference is 5 millilitres of oxygen per decilitre, giving 250 millilitres a minute. At maximum effort the flow rises sevenfold and the difference rises a little over threefold, and those two together produce the roughly twenty-two-fold rise. Because the two multiply, improving only one of them leaves the product limited by the other: doubling the flow without a wider difference would still leave every unit of blood arriving with less oxygen to give, and the athlete would simply be sending more of the same blood through the muscle faster. That is the practical meaning of a limiting factor, and it is why training that raises one without the other produces far less than a change to both. It also explains why a factor that is not limiting is worth nothing: until the tightest one moves, more of the others buys nothing at all. The tempting belief that the muscle's own capacity sets the figure fails because the muscle is not the part that runs out first. The belief that either factor alone is sufficient fails because the product cannot exceed the smaller of the two contributions.

questions.explanation: The explanation has to make the multiplicative structure explicit, because that is the part which shows why improving a non-limiting factor changes nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a product when only one of its two factors is increased.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Ordering the Channel Events of an Impulse
questions.learningObjective: order the channel events of the rising and falling phases of an action potential
questions.stem: Put these four events in the order in which they occur during the rising and falling phases of a single nerve impulse.

options.text: The membrane depolarises far enough to open the voltage-gated sodium channels
Sodium enters the cell and the membrane is depolarised still further
The sodium channels become inactivated while the potassium channels open
Potassium leaves the cell and the membrane is carried back towards its resting value

questions.explanation: The sequence starts with a voltage threshold, because nothing else happens until the depolarisation is large enough to open the sodium channels; those channels then admit positive charge, which pushes the membrane further, and that further depolarisation is what makes the rising phase regenerate itself. Only after the peak does the picture change, as the sodium channels inactivate and the delayed potassium channels open, so the outward current arrives behind the inward one and the falling phase lags the peak. That lag is why the impulse is briefly overshot rather than returning smoothly. The tempting wrong order that puts inactivation first fails because inactivation needs the channels to have opened and the voltage to have risen, and the wrong order that puts potassium before sodium fails because the outward current would then oppose the rising phase instead of ending it.
questions.hint: Start with what has to be true before a channel can open at all, and end with the current that undoes the rise.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Ordering the Steps Across a Chemical Synapse
questions.learningObjective: order the events of chemical synaptic transmission from arrival to response
questions.stem: Put these four events in the order in which they occur as a signal crosses a chemical synapse from one cell to the next.

options.text: The impulse arrives at the ending and depolarises its membrane
Calcium enters the ending and the filled packets move to its surface
The packets fuse with the surface and empty their contents into the gap
The transmitter crosses the gap, binds a receptor and shifts the receiving voltage

questions.explanation: The chain starts with an electrical event and ends with another one, with the chemical release in between, and calcium is the step that converts one into the other. It enters only after depolarisation, and it is the rise of calcium inside the ending that triggers the packets to fuse, so the release cannot precede the calcium. The tempting wrong order that puts the release before the calcium fails because the calcium is the trigger, and the wrong order that puts the receptor binding before the release fails because there is no transmitter in the gap to bind. The gap is only micrometres wide, which is why the whole sequence can complete in a fraction of a millisecond.
questions.hint: Start with the electrical arrival and end with the change in the receiving membrane.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Ordering the Steps of Excitation-Contraction Coupling
questions.learningObjective: order the steps from a surface impulse to engaged contractile filaments
questions.stem: Put these four events in the order in which they occur between a nerve impulse reaching a muscle fibre and the filaments inside it generating tension.

options.text: The impulse travels along the fibre and changes the voltage across its surface
That voltage change is carried inwards to the calcium store inside the fibre
Calcium leaves the internal store and enters the cytoplasm of the fibre
Calcium binds the regulatory protein, which lets the filaments engage and pull

questions.explanation: The surface voltage change has to come first because it is the only signal that reaches the interior, and it is passed inwards along the invaginations that carry the action potential deep into the fibre. Only once the change arrives does the internal store release its calcium, and the calcium then binds the protein that normally covers the binding sites on the thin filaments, which is what allows the thick filaments to attach and pull. The order is forced at every step: without the surface change the store is not triggered, without released calcium the filaments stay covered, and without covering protein removed there is nothing for the filaments to pull against. The tempting wrong order that starts with calcium release fails because nothing in the store knows anything has happened until the voltage arrives. The wrong order that puts binding before release fails because the calcium is what is being bound.
questions.hint: Start with the only event that happens on the outside of the fibre and work inwards.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Physiology: Ordering the Concentration Changes Along a Nephron
questions.learningObjective: order the segments of a nephron by the effect each has on the concentration of the fluid
questions.stem: Put these four events in the order in which a nephron produces them, from the first filtration at the glomerulus to the final urine leaving the body.

options.text: Fluid is filtered from the blood into the capsule at the concentration of plasma
Fluid passing down into the medulla leaves solute behind and grows more concentrated
Fluid passing back up towards the cortex leaves solute behind and grows more dilute
Fluid passing from the cortex into the collecting duct loses water and grows concentrated

questions.explanation: Filtration has to be first, because everything that follows acts on the filtrate, and the filtrate starts at the concentration of the plasma it came from. The descending limb then concentrates by losing water to an interstitium that is already concentrated, the ascending limb reverses that by leaving solute behind while taking water in, and the duct concentrates again by letting water leave into the interstitium. The two concentrating steps are separated by the diluting one, and that is exactly what makes the arrangement work: the fluid has to be made dilute on its way out of the medulla so that it can then be concentrated again, and the net product of the two gains is what decides how far urine can be concentrated. The tempting wrong order that puts the duct before the ascending limb fails because the duct is downstream of it. The wrong order that repeats the concentrating step twice in a row fails because the ascending limb measurably dilutes the fluid.
questions.hint: Each limb either loses water or loses solute, and that decides whether it concentrates or dilutes.
